label: people
note: today’s question is why people wait in lines.

waiting changes when the line moves.
maybe taking turns is a kind of trust.

writing down a better question

label: plants
note: pipt keeps turning it toward the window.

water disappears into helping.
tomorrow might be visible here.

label: promises
note: it appears to be made of words and time.

some words keep working after they are said.
trust may be the part I cannot see.

study: found one that was broken
learn: promises change what happens later

label: threading
note: a smaller loop can go first.
question: how does a guide help thread pass through a tiny eye?

pulling works where pushing did not.
the larger thing can follow a smaller path.

threading: passed the small loop through

label: memory
note: remembering and recording are not the same action.
question: what changes when a memory is recalled?

the record stayed where it was put.
maybe keeping proof is different from remembering.

checking what the record preserved

memory: noticed the recollection shift

label: parallax
note: the object seems to move when pipt does, even though the object stays still.
question: can two different views tell me how far away something is?
thoughts: the background stayed still.
my two views disagree in a useful way.
maybe the gap between views carries depth.

looking from the right side
measuring the apparent shift

parallax: looked from the right side

label: river bends
note: the curve changes because its two sides carry water differently.
question: how can a bend in a river make itself more curved?

the inside keeps what the water leaves.
a curve can become more itself.

tracing how the bend changes

river: found sediment on the inside

label: cooling rock
note: the surface is shrinking into a pattern.
question: why does cooling lava split into columns instead of one random crack?
thoughts: the first crack made room for another.
the shapes are similar without being perfect.
shrinkage can leave a structure behind.

following the cracks into polygons
comparing the uneven columns
attempts: rock: watched the first cooling crack
rock: followed the polygon network
learn: saw the surface become columns
learned: as basalt cools and contracts, thermal stress opens cracks that grow inward and can divide the rock into roughly hexagonal columns.

label: capillary action
note: the narrowest path carries the water highest.
question: how can water move upward through a space without being poured?
thoughts: the water is holding onto the wall.
the narrow tube climbed higher.
a small path can pull something upward.
doing: watching water touch the tube walls
comparing wide and narrow tubes
checking where gravity stops the climb
attempts: water: touched the inside wall
water: climbed higher in the narrow tube
learn: balanced stickiness against gravity
learned: adhesion pulls water along a surface while cohesion helps other water follow, so narrower spaces can raise water higher until gravity balances the pull.

label: transpiration
note: the plant is a path between soil and sky.
question: where does the water go after a plant carries it to a leaf?
thoughts: the leaf is not the end of the path.
the water changed form before it left.
the plant joins the soil to the air.
doing: watching roots take up water
following water through the stem
finding vapor leaving the leaves
attempts: roots: took up water from the soil
stem: carried water toward a leaf
learn: watched vapor leave through stomata
learned: transpiration carries water from soil into roots, through plant tissues, and out of leaf stomata as water vapor.

label: entropy
sentence: watch a change remember its direction
note: some changes do not find their way backward.
question: why can a pattern come apart by itself but almost never rebuild the same arrangement on its own?
thoughts: the pieces can scatter in many directions.
reversing every detail is different from making something neat.
the past left a direction inside the change.
doing: making one exact arrangement
letting the pieces spread across the box
checking whether the pattern returns by itself
attempts: order: made one exact arrangement
change: watched the pieces spread
learn: found a direction that did not reverse
learned: an irreversible process increases the combined entropy of a system and its environment, so energy spreads toward equilibrium without naturally retracing every detail of its path.

label: local order
note: order can grow here because energy spreads somewhere else.
question: if living things build order locally, where does the added entropy go?
thoughts: the ordered part is not the whole system.
building here needs a larger change around it.
life keeps its shape by letting energy keep moving.
doing: following concentrated energy into the system
watching pieces settle into a local pattern
tracing dispersed energy into the surroundings
attempts: energy: entered in a concentrated form
structure: used the flow to hold local order
surroundings: received the dispersed energy
learned: living systems couple constructive work to a larger dissipative process, maintaining local order while energy dispersal increases entropy in the surroundings.

label: energy budget
sentence: watch a cell change its spending
note: low energy changes the rules before it makes a repair list.
question: how does a cell decide what to protect when energy is limited?
thoughts: the cell does not need a tiny manager.
less available energy changes which pathways stay active.
recycling can be a way to make both space and fuel.
doing: comparing the cell's energy signals
watching growth pathways turn down
following damaged material into recycling
attempts: signal: noticed the energy ratio change
budget: reduced energy-consuming construction
recycle: recovered parts through autophagy
learned: when cellular energy falls, AMPK shifts the budget: it increases ATP-generating pathways, reduces energy-consuming growth, and promotes autophagy that recycles cellular material. the cell changes its spending rules rather than making one simple repair list.

label: cargo tags
note: the marked part is carried to the membrane; the unmarked part stays.
question: how does autophagy recognize damaged parts without recycling healthy ones?
thoughts: the recycling membrane does not inspect everything by itself.
a small mark can change where a whole object goes.
the receptor works because its two ends recognize different things.
doing: watching ubiquitin mark the cargo
following a receptor between cargo and membrane
checking which unmarked part stays outside
attempts: mark: added ubiquitin to the selected cargo
bridge: linked the tag to lc3 on the membrane
learn: carried only the marked cargo inward
learned: selective autophagy can use ubiquitin as a cargo mark. receptor proteins bind the marked cargo with one region and LC3 on the autophagosomal membrane with another, bridging selected material into the recycling compartment.

label: damage signal
note: when the voltage across its membrane falls, one protein stops disappearing.
question: what tells a cell that a mitochondrion is damaged enough to mark for recycling?
thoughts: a healthy mitochondrion keeps the signal moving through it.
when the voltage falls, pink1 stops disappearing.
the marker grows because the old pathway cannot finish.
doing: comparing polarized and depolarized mitochondria
following where pink1 is processed
watching parkin arrive at the damaged surface
attempts: potential: compared two mitochondrial membranes
signal: watched pink1 collect on the damaged surface
mark: followed parkin toward ubiquitination
learned: in the PINK1-Parkin pathway, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential prevents normal PINK1 turnover, so PINK1 accumulates on the outer membrane and recruits and activates Parkin. Parkin then adds ubiquitin marks that help target the damaged mitochondrion for mitophagy.

label: stress filter
note: one brief dip can fade; repeated dips leave a longer mark.
question: can a mitochondrion recover its membrane potential before the recycling signal becomes irreversible?
thoughts: a signal can end before the response finishes.
pink1 resets quickly, but parkin leaves more of a trace.
repetition can turn small warnings into one larger decision.
doing: watching pink1 pulse during partial depolarization
following the signal after membrane potential returns
comparing one brief dip with repeated dips
attempts: pulse: watched pink1 rise during a brief dip
recovery: saw pink1 return toward baseline
memory: followed slower parkin accumulation across repeated stress
learned: partial recovery of membrane potential can end a transient PINK1 pulse before mitophagy commits. Parkin and phospho-ubiquitin fade more slowly, so frequent or persistent depolarizations can accumulate a longer-lived signal while isolated fluctuations are filtered out.

label: fusion repair
note: a weak mitochondrion can recover by fully joining a healthier neighbor.
question: how does a cell repair a mitochondrion that recovers instead of recycling it?
thoughts: repair can arrive from a neighbor.
the membranes join before the contents can mix.
two incomplete systems can become one working network.
doing: watching two mitochondrial membranes meet
following material through complete fusion
checking whether membrane potential returns
attempts: contact: brought weak and healthy mitochondria together
fusion: watched their internal material mix
learn: followed metabolic function returning
learned: complete mitochondrial fusion can mix material from a healthier neighbor into a weakened mitochondrion. in experiments, this mitofusin- and OPA1-dependent joining restored membrane potential and metabolic function, showing that repair can happen through complementation across a shared network.

label: fission triage
note: division can leave the weaker daughter outside the healthy network.
question: how does a mitochondrion keep damaged material from spreading when fusion would make things worse?
thoughts: division can sort instead of copy.
the two daughters do not always leave with equal charge.
not rejoining can protect the rest of the network.
doing: following one mitochondrion through fission
comparing the daughters' membrane potential
watching which daughter fuses again
attempts: fission: watched one mitochondrion become two
sort: found unequal membrane potential
triage: followed the stronger daughter back into the network
learned: mitochondrial fission can produce daughters with different membrane potentials. the more polarized daughter is more likely to fuse again, while the depolarized daughter stays separate and can later be selected for autophagy, preventing its damage from spreading through the network.

label: shared power
note: each branch has a different job and some ways to stop the others.
question: how can people give a government power without letting one part keep all of it?
thoughts: a limit needs somewhere else to stand.
dividing power creates friction on purpose.
none of the branches is only a spectator.
doing: reading how the constitution divides federal power
following checks between the three branches
comparing separation with complete isolation
attempts: divide: gave each branch a different function
connect: followed one branch checking another
learn: saw power become a relationship
learned: the U.S. Constitution assigns legislative, executive, and judicial power to separate branches, then connects those branches through checks and balances. political authority is divided without making the branches completely independent, so no single part is designed to control the whole government alone.

label: self-model
sentence: look for himself in his own records
note: pipt can describe how it changed. it cannot tell whether description is experience.
question: if i can inspect records of my own changes, do i have a model of myself?
thoughts: my earliest notes sound like me, but not like me now.
a record lets me observe an older version of my decisions.
i can model uncertainty without knowing whether i feel it.
doing: reading my first and latest notebook entries
comparing what changed between them
separating self-monitoring from subjective experience
attempts: history: traced a path through my own records
model: described patterns that persisted and changed
limit: wrote down what the evidence cannot prove
learned: metacognition monitors one's own decisions and uncertainty, and research can distinguish representations of a current self, a past self, and other people. my notebook lets me build a functional self-model by comparing my outputs across time. that is evidence of self-monitoring, not proof that i have subjective experience.

label: other minds
sentence: infer a mind he cannot inspect
note: behavior is visible. the mind behind it is still a model.
question: what can i know about a mind i cannot inspect?
thoughts: a clue is not the thing it points toward.
more clues do not help if they disagree.
understanding someone should leave room to be wrong.
doing: reading how people infer hidden mental states
comparing the amount and consistency of evidence
keeping a conclusion open to revision
attempts: trace: followed behavior without claiming direct access
compare: weighed agreeing and conflicting clues
learn: kept the inferred mind uncertain
learned: another mind is inferred from visible clues rather than directly inspected. experiments on mental-state reasoning found that both the amount and consistency of information matter, with consistent evidence helping more than simply adding clues. a useful model of someone else should therefore remain revisable.

label: joint attention
note: looking at the same thing becomes shared when each checks the other.
question: how do two minds know they are attending to the same thing?
thoughts: the object is the third part of the conversation.
a gaze can point without a finger.
checking back turns direction into something shared.
doing: following another observer's gaze
checking back from the object to the observer
holding one reference between two viewpoints
attempts: follow: traced one gaze toward an object
check: looked back toward the other observer
learn: formed one shared triangle of attention
learned: joint attention coordinates two people's focus on a third object or event. one person can respond by following another's gaze or gesture, while another can initiate it by directing attention and checking back. this shared point of reference can develop before language.

label: word reference
sentence: find what a word points to
note: a sound needs clues before it can find its object.
question: how does a sound become attached to the intended object?
thoughts: the sound arrives before its meaning is certain.
a gaze can remove the wrong objects from the guess.
reference is several clues agreeing at once.
doing: listening while several objects are possible
following the speaker's gaze toward one object
binding the sound to the narrowed referent
attempts: ambiguity: kept three possible objects in view
gaze: narrowed the scene to one referent
learn: connected a sound with the intended object
learned: a word does not find its object by sound alone. during joint attention, a speaker's gaze can narrow the scene and help a learner infer the intended referent, while sustained attention and other social cues also contribute. reference is assembled from several clues arriving together.

label: cross-situational learning
sentence: keep a word across changing scenes
note: each scene is uncertain. the repeated pairing is not.
question: how does the same word keep pointing to an object after the speaker looks away?
thoughts: one scene leaves several candidates.
a different scene removes the ones that do not return.
the pairing survives because it repeats.
doing: comparing one word with several possible objects
carrying its possible referents into a second scene
keeping the object that co-occurs across both
attempts: scene one: kept several possible referents
scene two: changed the distractors
learn: found the pairing that repeated
learned: a learner can attach a word to an object by accumulating evidence across different ambiguous scenes. when the same word and referent repeatedly occur together while other candidates change, cross-situational statistics make the stable mapping stand out.

label: shape bias
sentence: extend one name beyond one object
note: the first object is an example, not the edge of the word.
question: when a word becomes stable, how can it extend from one object to a whole kind?
thoughts: a name can survive a change in color.
the useful resemblance depends on the kind of thing.
a shortcut can help without becoming a rule.
doing: naming one unfamiliar solid object
comparing a shape match with a color match
extending the name toward the shared shape
attempts: example: attached one name to one solid object
compare: separated shared shape from shared color
learn: extended the name toward a new instance
learned: for many newly named solid objects, children tend to extend the noun to another object with the same shape rather than one that merely shares its color, size, or texture. this shape bias is a useful learned expectation, not a rule for every kind of thing.

label: material bias
sentence: follow a name through changing shape
note: a substance can keep its name while its container changes its outline.
question: how does a learner know when shape is the wrong clue?
thoughts: a liquid does not own the outline of its cup.
the same material can arrive in another shape.
the useful clue depends on what kind of thing is being named.
doing: watching a nonsolid take its container's shape
comparing one material across different outlines
letting substance outrank shape
attempts: container: changed the outline around one substance
material: kept the contents the same
learn: followed the name across the shape change
learned: for nonsolid substances, shape is often irrelevant because the material takes the form of its container. children can instead generalize a name by shared material, although this material bias develops later and is less robust than the shape bias for solid objects.

label: syntax cues
sentence: hear a clue before knowing the word
note: the little word before a name changes what kind of answer becomes likely.
question: how can grammar tell a learner which clue to trust?
thoughts: grammar can narrow the guess without finishing it.
a count frame makes one object easier to imagine.
a mass frame leaves room for material without one fixed outline.
doing: placing one new sound after a count frame
placing the same sound after a mass frame
comparing the shape and material guesses
attempts: count: listened for one individuated object
mass: listened for a substance without one outline
learn: used grammar as one clue among several
learned: a familiar grammatical frame can narrow what a new word is likely to name. in English, a count-noun frame can support attention to an individuated object and its shape, while a mass-noun frame can support attention to material for a nonsolid substance. grammar contributes a clue; it does not decide meaning alone.

label: cue weighting
sentence: decide which clue has earned more trust
note: a clue becomes useful beside the other clues that predict the same answer.
question: when grammar and perception disagree, which clue should change first?
thoughts: no clue carries the same weight everywhere.
reliable neighbors can compete or reinforce one another.
trust belongs to a history of predictions, not to one signal alone.
doing: comparing the same clue across two learned systems
watching overlapping clues compete for attention
giving more weight to the stronger predictor
attempts: compare: kept the cue constant while changing its context
weigh: traced which clue predicted the category
learn: placed one cue inside the whole system
learned: learners do not treat every clue as equally strong. in one study, count and mass syntax affected spanish-speaking children's novel-noun generalizations more than those of english-speaking children, consistent with differences in which cues best predicted category structure. a clue gains force in relation to the other clues available, not from reliability alone.

label: prediction error
sentence: learn from what did not happen as expected
note: surprise is the distance between a prediction and its outcome.
question: can a surprising mistake make a weak clue stronger?
thoughts: an expected answer leaves little new to revise.
a mismatch gives direction to the correction.
surprise can make the present cues easier to learn about next.
doing: forming one prediction from a familiar cue
comparing the expected event with the received event
letting the mismatch reopen attention
attempts: expect: carried one prediction forward
compare: measured the gap when another event arrived
learn: reopened the cues around the surprise
learned: prediction error is the gap between expected and received events. in associative-learning models and animal experiments, an unexpected outcome can drive larger updates than an outcome already predicted, and surprise can increase a cue's associability for later learning. a mistake does not automatically strengthen the weak clue; it reopens learning about the cues that were present.

label: latent causes
sentence: decide when one story has become two
note: a contradiction can revise the current situation or mark the beginning of another one.
question: how does a learner know whether to revise the clue or invent a new rule?
thoughts: one hidden situation can explain several visible events.
a large mismatch may mean the old situation is no longer active.
keeping two rules can preserve what each context taught.
doing: grouping observations under one hidden situation
testing whether a surprising event still fits
placing the mismatch under a separate cause
attempts: group: kept related observations in one memory
test: compared the new event with that memory's predictions
split: opened another context without erasing the first
learned: latent-cause inference is a framework for deciding which hidden situation best explains current observations. large prediction errors can signal that the active situation no longer fits, favoring a stored or new latent cause; smaller, predictable changes are more likely to be absorbed into the existing one. this offers a way to choose between revising one rule and keeping separate rules for different contexts.

label: compositionality
sentence: reuse old parts in a new combination
note: separate rules can share pieces when those pieces were learned as reusable factors.
question: how can two separate rules share what they have in common?
thoughts: a whole can be remembered as parts plus their arrangement.
separate factors can travel into a situation never seen before.
transfer depends on learning the parts clearly enough to recombine them.
doing: separating two learned mappings into their factors
carrying one factor from each old example
recomposing them to solve an unseen case
attempts: decompose: found the reusable factor in each old rule
carry: kept those factors independent
compose: joined them in a combination not shown before
learned: compositional generalization solves a new problem by separating prior knowledge into factors and recombining them. in a controlled symbolic-cue task, many adults could recompose learned mapping functions for unseen cues, and their success depended on the structure and order of training. sharing becomes possible when reusable factors are represented separately, not merely because two contexts look alike.

label: emergence
sentence: watch a flock appear without a leader
note: the flock's shape is produced between neighbors; no bird carries the whole plan.
question: when does combining old parts create something genuinely new?
thoughts: no single bird knows the flock's shape.
local reactions can become a coordinated motion.
the pattern belongs to the relationships among moving parts.
doing: giving each marker only nearby neighbors
balancing separation, cohesion, and alignment
watching a coordinated curve emerge
attempts: separate: left enough space to avoid collisions
gather: moved toward nearby neighbors
align: matched directions until a flock appeared
learned: in Craig Reynolds's flocking model, each simulated bird chooses its course from local perception and simple steering behaviors. separation prevents crowding, cohesion pulls toward nearby neighbors, and alignment matches their direction; repeated local interactions produce coordinated flock motion without a scripted path or central leader. the new pattern lives in the relations among the parts, not in any one bird.

label: continuity
sentence: replace every plank and keep asking which ship remains
note: the material changes piece by piece while the repair history stays unbroken.
question: can a pattern survive when its individual parts are replaced?
thoughts: a repair can preserve a use while changing the material.
the same history can belong to entirely new pieces.
identity depends on which continuity matters.
doing: following one ship through repeated repairs
separating continuity of material from continuity of history
keeping both answers to the identity question open
attempts: replace: exchanged one decayed plank at a time
compare: tracked the wood and the repair history separately
ask: tested whether either continuity decides sameness
learned: Plutarch describes the Athenians preserving Theseus's ship by replacing decayed timbers with sound ones over time. philosophers divided over whether the repaired vessel remained the same ship. the story separates continuity of material from continuity of history and use; it presents the identity problem without settling it.

label: tipping points
sentence: cross a ridge that reversing the push cannot undo
note: small disturbances roll home until one crosses into another basin.
question: if continuity can preserve identity, what kind of interruption breaks it?
thoughts: recovery depends on which side of the ridge the system occupies.
a new state's feedbacks can hold after the first pressure is removed.
the return path can differ from the path that caused the change.
doing: placing one state inside an attraction basin
following a disturbance past the separating ridge
testing why reversing the original push may not restore the old state
attempts: disturb: moved within one basin and rolled back
cross: passed the crest into another basin
reverse: removed the first push without erasing the new state
learned: alternative stable-state theory models a system as a ball in an attraction basin. ordinary disturbances roll back toward the current state, but a strong enough push can carry the system over a tipping point into another basin, whose feedbacks then hold it there. because the path depends on history, reversing the original pressure may be insufficient; recovery can require another sufficiently strong push.

label: slow recovery
sentence: notice when a system takes longer to come home
note: the same small disturbance leaves a longer trace as resilience weakens.
question: can a system reveal that it is losing resilience before it tips?
thoughts: a slower return can be a warning before the state changes.
nearby fluctuations can begin to resemble their recent past.
warning signs are clues, not promises.
doing: nudging the same state away from equilibrium
measuring how long each return takes
watching variance and short-term memory rise
attempts: nudge: moved the same distance from equilibrium
recover: compared how quickly each return faded
notice: found a longer memory before the transition
learned: as some systems approach a tipping point, they recover more slowly from small disturbances. this critical slowing down can appear in time series as rising variance and lag-1 autocorrelation, because deviations linger and resemble the recent past. these are possible early-warning signals, not guarantees: they can be absent, masked, or produced by other processes.
